Who bills and collects property tax

In New Hampshire the city or town does all of it. Each municipality assesses the property, sets the rate and collects the money under RSA 76 and the Rev 600 rules. The state does not send homeowners a bill. The Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) watches assessing practices, reviews municipal records and oversees revaluations, but it is not who you pay.

When you sell, you will deal with two local offices. The assessor answers value questions. The tax collector gives payoff figures and tells you whether a lien exists. Two houses that sell for the same price in neighboring towns can carry very different bills, because each town picks its own rate.

The property tax year runs from April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), and taxes are based on the inventory taken in April. A fall sale does not change that: the April 1 assessment still drives the bills that arrive afterward, so work out the split with your closing attorney or title company before you sign.

Due dates and interest

Towns and cities that bill twice a year follow RSA 76:15-a. A partial payment is due July 1 and the balance is due December 1.

  • The July bill is built from the prior year's assessed value times one-half of the previous year's tax rate.
  • Assessors commit the lists to the collector by May 15, and the partial-payment bills go out no later than June 15.
  • The December bill is whatever remains of the taxes assessed April 1, minus the July payment.

Not every municipality uses that pattern. Concord, for one, sends four quarterly bills in July, October, January and March, based on the prior April 1 assessment. The due dates printed on your own bill are the ones that count, so read it or call your collector.

Interest runs at 8 percent per annum on taxes not paid by December 1 after assessment (RSA 76:13). Hampton's town page describes the same 8 percent rate, counted daily from the day after a bill is due.

What happens if the taxes are not paid?

An unpaid bill can turn into a tax lien, and a lien nobody redeems can end in a tax deed. This is the collection chapter, RSA 80, and it applies in municipalities that use the lien procedure.

  • The collector must send notice of the impending lien at least 30 days before executing it, by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested (RSA 80:60).
  • Only the municipality, the county or the state can hold a tax lien on land and buildings (RSA 80:63).
  • Anyone with a legal interest in the land can redeem by paying the lien amount plus interest at 14 percent per annum from the execution date, at any point before the collector gives a deed (RSA 80:69).
  • Once 2 years pass from execution of an unredeemed lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder (RSA 80:76).

The jump from 8 to 14 percent is where owners start to feel real pressure. If you are behind and thinking about selling, plan on the redemption payment coming out of your proceeds at closing. A municipality may also refuse a tax deed, in which case the lien stays in place and the right of redemption continues.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin with a written abatement application to your town's selectmen or assessors. The deadline is March 1 after the date on your notice of tax (RSA 76:16), and the form comes from the Board of Tax and Land Appeals (BTLA). You must have complied with the RSA 74 inventory requirement, and the application has to give specific reasons and list any comparable properties. A vague complaint about the amount rarely goes anywhere, so bring numbers.

Abatement and appeal deadlines
StepDeadline
Apply for abatement with the municipalityMarch 1 after the notice of tax
Municipality decides in writingJuly 1 after the notice of tax date; no response counts as denial
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax on or before Dec. 31September 1, but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1
Appeal to BTLA, notice of tax after Dec. 318 months after the notice of tax
BTLA filing fee$65, check or money order to Treasurer, State of NH

An abatement is a request for a refund of taxes because of a physical description error, damage to a building during the tax year, or a difference of opinion on value. If the town turns you down, the next step can be an appeal to BTLA or to Superior Court.

Exemptions and credits

New Hampshire offers several exemptions and military-service credits, and nothing is applied unless the owner asks. The permanent application, Form PA-29, goes to the municipal assessing officials by April 15, before the tax rate is set. They respond by July 1. No response counts as a denial, which can be appealed to BTLA or Superior Court by September 1 after the notice of tax.

  • Elderly exemption (RSA 72:39-a): the applicant must be 65 by April 1 and a New Hampshire resident for three consecutive years, and income and asset limits apply.
  • Blind exemption (RSA 72:37): $15,000 off the assessed value unless the town votes more.
  • Standard service credit (RSA 72:28): $50 standard, and towns can adopt $51 up to $750.
  • Service-connected total disability credit (RSA 72:35): $700 standard, and towns can adopt up to $5,000.
  • Disabled exemption (RSA 72:37-b): only where the town has adopted it.

The qualifying date is April 1 of the tax year. Exemptions belong to a person and a home, so a buyer applies for their own. If you sell and move before the next April 1, ask the assessing office how that affects any credit you hold.

Selling with taxes owed

Before closing day, find out from the tax collector exactly what is owed, including any lien amount. Ask for a written payoff figure and for confirmation of whether a lien has been executed on the parcel.

  • Pull your most recent bill, and the previous year's if any part is unpaid.
  • Ask whether a notice of impending lien has been sent, and when interest started.
  • If a lien exists, ask for the redemption amount through the expected closing date, since interest at 14 percent per annum keeps running.
  • Plan for the transfer tax: $.75 per $100 of the price from the seller and the same from the buyer, paid with stamps bought from the register of deeds.

When back taxes, a lien and needed repairs all pile up, an as-is cash sale can be a cleaner way out, because the buyer does not wait on a lender's appraisal. No price or timeline is promised here. Talk with your collector and a New Hampshire attorney for your exact numbers.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in New Hampshire?

Your city or town does. Municipalities assess, levy and collect under RSA 76, and the state Department of Revenue Administration monitors assessing practices.

When are New Hampshire property taxes due?

In towns that bill twice a year, a partial payment is due July 1 and the balance December 1. Some municipalities bill quarterly, so follow the dates printed on your own bill.

What interest applies to late property taxes?

Eight percent per annum on taxes not paid by December 1 after assessment (RSA 76:13). After a lien is executed, redemption carries 14 percent per annum (RSA 80:69).

What is the deadline to ask for an abatement?

March 1 following the date of the notice of tax. The municipality must decide in writing by July 1, and no response is a denial. The BTLA filing fee is $65.

Can I sell a house that has a tax lien?

Yes. A person with a legal interest can redeem by paying the lien amount plus 14 percent per annum before the collector gives a deed, and in a sale that payoff is usually handled from the proceeds at closing.

New Hampshire Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Hampshire?

Homestead right versus property tax exemptions

The New Hampshire homestead right is a creditor protection under RSA chapter 480. It shields up to $400,000 of a person's homestead, or of their interest in it, and it is separate from the property tax exemptions that towns grant. Many people search for a "homestead exemption" expecting a tax break, as in other states. Here, tax relief comes from different statutes and is set town by town.

A selling homeowner will run into both. The homestead right matters when a creditor, a lien or sale proceeds are in play. The property tax exemptions matter when a bill is due or an application has to move with you to a new home.

How much the homestead right protects

RSA 480:1 entitles every person to $400,000 worth of their homestead or their interest in it.

FeatureRule under RSA 480:1
Amount$400,000 per person
Property typesIncludes manufactured housing you own and occupy, mobile homes, housing cooperatives and condominiums, if occupied as a dwelling
Occupancy testPrimary residence continuously for the previous 12 months
Sale proceedsProtected if reinvested within 6 months in a new primary residence
Combined ceilingParagraph III sets a total of not more than $550,000, or $400,000 for a single person
Medical debtFull market value may be claimed for debts from terminal or catastrophic injury or illness
TrustsA beneficiary of a qualifying trust that owns the property may claim it

The text is at RSA 480:1. It protects equity from creditors. It does nothing for your tax bill.

When does the homestead right not protect the house?

RSA 480:4 makes clear that the homestead right erases no debt, and it lists the cases where protection does not apply. The list helps a seller judge whether a lien will follow the sale.

  • The collection of taxes.
  • Liens to collect on forfeited bail bonds or domestic support obligations.
  • Liens of mechanics and others for debts created in constructing, repairing or improving the homestead.
  • Enforcement of mortgages made a charge on the property as the law provides.
  • Liens filed by homeowner associations or by condominium associations under RSA 356-B for unpaid assessments, including collection costs.
  • Debts that existed when the homestead was purchased, unless the reinvestment rule in RSA 480:1, II applies.
  • The levy of executions as provided in the chapter.

A homestead claim will not hold off a mortgage lender or a tax collector. It is aimed at ordinary unsecured creditors.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens to the homestead right when I sell?

Sale proceeds stay protected only if you reinvest them in a new primary residence within 6 months (RSA 480:1, II). If you take cash from the sale and do not buy another primary residence inside that window, do not assume the money still carries the shield.

The 12-month rule works the other way when you buy. To claim the homestead right in a new house, it must have been your primary residence continuously for the previous 12 months. The reinvestment clause is the exception that carries protection from the old house to the new one.

If you are selling because of debt, talk to a New Hampshire attorney before closing.

Property tax exemptions and credits

Towns and cities grant property tax exemptions and credits under RSA chapter 72, and the dollar amounts differ by municipality. Local property taxes are assessed, levied and collected by the municipality under RSA 76. As one example of what a city can adopt, Manchester grants the following:

  • Elderly exemption under RSA 72:39-a, with assessed value deducted of $240,000 for ages 65 to 74, $325,000 for ages 75 to 79 and $435,000 for age 80 and over.
  • Blind exemption of $240,000 assessed value.
  • Disabled exemption of $240,000 assessed value.
  • Military service credit of $500 toward taxes due, with a $2,000 credit for those disabled in service and $2,000 for surviving spouses.
  • Tax deferral, with total deferrals limited to 85 percent of assessed value.

Another town may adopt different numbers, so read your own town's assessing page.

The elderly exemption

The elderly exemption requires three consecutive years of New Hampshire residence before April 1 of the year you claim it, plus income and asset limits the town or city sets (RSA 72:39-a). The statute puts floors under those limits: not less than $13,400 net income for a single person or $20,400 for married persons, and not less than $35,000 in net assets, excluding the person's residence and its land up to the greater of 2 acres or the minimum single-family lot size.

RSA 72:39-b adds age brackets. A town may grant a different dollar amount at 65 up to 75, 75 up to 80, and 80 or older, and the exemption cannot be less than $5,000 in any category. Someone married to an owner for at least 5 consecutive years can qualify through the spouse's ownership. When an owner dies, the combined net asset amount for married persons continues to apply to the surviving spouse until the property is sold or transferred, or until the surviving spouse remarries.

How and when to apply

File a permanent application with your town's selectmen or assessors by April 15 before the tax rate is set, on the state form (RSA 72:33). You sign it under penalty of perjury, and it shows that you own the property and were qualified on April 1 of the first year.

The deadline has a safety valve. If accident, mistake or misfortune kept you from filing on time, the assessors may accept a late application, but not after the local tax rate has been approved for that year.

  • One filing normally carries forward each year as long as you do not change residence.
  • Assessors can ask you to re-qualify no more than once a year, and failing to respond can cost you the exemption for that year. In Manchester, existing exemptions continue automatically but are subject to annual re-qualification or audit.

If the town denies your exemption

Appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or to superior court, no later than September 1 following the notice of tax (RSA 72:34-a). The BTLA form needs a nonrefundable $65 check payable to the Treasurer, State of New Hampshire.

If your town bills twice a year, the notice of tax date is the final bill that sets your tax liability, so you appeal after that bill and not before. This appeal covers only the exemption. An appeal of the assessment itself is a separate filing under RSA 76:16.

Your exemption when you sell

Tell the assessor. An exemption attaches to your qualifying residence and does not travel with the sale. RSA 72:33, II requires a person who changes residence after filing a permanent application to file an amended permanent application by December 1 following the move. In Manchester, owners who hold an elderly exemption or military service credit and are selling or moving are asked to say so, so the exemption can be applied to the new home.

The tax year matters at closing. It runs April 1 to March 31, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken in April (RSA 76:2). Towns that bill semiannually send a partial payment bill due July 1 and the remainder due December 1 (RSA 76:15-a). Your closing agent will prorate the current bill, so ask the town for the amount and status before the sale.

Our team buys New Hampshire houses as-is, and we can talk through timing around a tax bill if you call.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does New Hampshire have a homestead exemption for property taxes?

Not under that name. The homestead right in RSA chapter 480 protects up to $400,000 of equity from creditors. Property tax relief comes from separate exemptions and credits under RSA 72, which each town or city adopts and sets.

How much is the New Hampshire homestead right worth?

It is $400,000 per person under RSA 480:1, with a combined ceiling of $550,000 stated in paragraph III.

What is the deadline to apply for a New Hampshire property tax exemption?

April 15 before the tax rate is set (RSA 72:33). The assessors can accept a late application for accident, mistake or misfortune, but not after the local tax rate has been approved for that year.

Can I keep my elderly exemption if I move?

Not automatically. You must file an amended permanent application by December 1 after the change of residence under RSA 72:33, II, and the new town's own limits and amounts will apply.

Are sale proceeds protected by the homestead right?

Proceeds from a qualifying residence are protected if reinvested within 6 months in a new primary residence (RSA 480:1, II).

New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

No estate or inheritance tax in New Hampshire

Neither one exists here. The inheritance tax, called the Legacy and Succession Tax, ended with deaths on or after January 1, 2003. The state estate tax return was dropped for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

The second change followed from the first federal one. New Hampshire's estate tax rode on a federal credit, and when Congress repealed that credit, the NH Estate Tax return lost its purpose. A third levy, the RSA 89 transfer tax on nonresident decedents' personal property, went away for those same 2003 deaths.

If you are an heir thinking about selling, no state death tax sits between you and the closing table. Other costs do apply, and they come next.

The old death taxes

The Legacy and Succession Tax was charged to certain heirs, not to the estate as one lump. It only matters today if you are settling a death from before 2003, which is rare but possible in an estate that has sat unsettled for decades.

TaxStatusApplies to deaths
Legacy and Succession Tax (RSA 86)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
Transfer tax on nonresident decedents' personal property (RSA 89)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
NH Estate Tax return (NH-706)Not requiredOn or after January 1, 2005

Back then, a return came due nine months after death. Close family (spouses, children, parents, grandparents, grandchildren) sat among the non-taxable legatees. Siblings, nieces, nephews, friends and other non-relatives sat among the taxable ones. The old NH-706 filing threshold was $675,000 for deaths in 2000 and 2001 and $1,000,000 for 2002 through 2004.

Does the federal estate tax matter for a house sale?

Rarely. A death in 2026 carries a $15,000,000 basic exclusion, and the same figure is the return filing threshold for that year.

Estates worth less than that generally owe no federal estate tax. A family selling a parent's home in New Hampshire is almost never affected.

  • Check the year of death, since the exclusion changes by year.
  • Count the whole estate, accounts and all, not only the house.
  • Close to the line? See an estate attorney before listing.

The IRS estate tax page posts each year's threshold, and the Form 706 instructions walk through the return for estates above it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Taxes an heir can still owe on an inherited house

Up to three charges can follow you into a sale: the state transfer tax, property tax, and possibly federal income tax on a gain. Receiving the house is different from selling it. When title passes by devise, by intestate succession or at a joint tenant's death, no transfer tax applies.

The resale is taxed at $0.75 per $100 of the price, with buyer and seller each covering a share. A price of $4,000 or less means a $20 minimum per side. Stamps come from the register of deeds in the county where the house sits.

The state wants the purchaser's and seller's declarations of consideration plus an Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) within 30 days of recording.

  1. Your half of the transfer tax on the sale
  2. Past-due property tax and any recorded lien
  3. Federal capital gain tax, when the price tops your basis (see our capital gains guide)

Inherited property gets its own basis treatment under IRS Publication 551. Your preparer can apply it to this house.

Probate and selling an inherited house

Whoever runs the estate signs the sale, with the Circuit Court Probate Division overseeing. Send probate questions to the Probate Court in the decedent's home county.

A will names an executor. With no will, or no named executor, the court appoints an administrator. Both are expected to seek the best price on any real estate or personal property they sell. If the sale is meant to cover debts or claims against the estate, the person in charge asks for a license on the Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Demands.

At the end, the executor files a final accounting on form NHJB-2117-Pe, the Executor's/Administrator's Accounting, and the duties are released.

Our New Hampshire probate guide goes through the court steps in more detail.

Who pays property tax on the house while the estate is open?

Taxes keep coming while the estate is open. The estate, or the heir who holds the house, is on the hook. With a tax year of April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), probate that drags on can mean two bills.

A late payment accrues 8 percent (RSA 76:13). After a lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 sets 14 percent a year, and anyone with a legal interest in the land can pay it off and redeem before the collector takes a deed.

  • Send the town or city assessing office your new mailing address.
  • Request a current payoff from the tax collector before you list.
  • Plan for delay: a new deed can take 30 days or more to reach the assessing office.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Hampshire houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps to sell an inherited house

Once you know no state death tax applies, the sale follows a fairly short path. Each step below reuses facts covered above.

  1. Confirm who has authority: the executor named in the will, or the administrator the court appointed.
  2. Collect the death certificate, the court appointment papers, the latest tax bill and any lien notices.
  3. Order an appraisal for the date of death, which your preparer will want for basis.
  4. Ask the tax collector for a payoff, and pay or plan to pay any past-due tax from the sale.
  5. If the sale is meant to pay debts or claims, ask the court for the license to sell.
  6. Close, buy the transfer tax stamps for your half, and file the declarations within 30 days after the deed is recorded.

Keep copies of every filing. When the estate is wrapped up, the executor needs them for the final accounting.

Who to call for answers

State tax questions go to the Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920, or by mail to NH DRA, Estate & Legacy, PO Box 457, Concord, NH 03302-0457. Ask them to confirm that a recent death needs no state return.

Wills, trusts and estates belong to the Probate Division of the Circuit Court. The case is filed in the county where the decedent lived.

Write down every answer you get. Before closing, the title company will ask for proof that the estate can sell and that taxes and liens are cleared.

Choices when you inherit a house you do not want

Options: hold it, rent it, list it, or sell as-is for cash. Taxes work the same under each, so the real tradeoffs are time and repair cost.

A cash sale as-is tends to fit estates with a worn-out house, unpaid taxes or heirs living out of state. The buyer takes the property as it stands, and the title company clears taxes and liens at closing. Price varies with every house and town, so we promise nothing here.

Start by collecting these papers:

  • The death certificate.
  • The will or the court appointment papers.
  • The latest tax bill.
  • Any lien notices.

With those in hand, a title company can say fast what stands between the estate and a closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does New Hampshire have an inheritance tax?

No. The Legacy and Succession Tax ended with deaths on or after January 1, 2003.

Is there a New Hampshire estate tax return to file?

Not for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. Repeal of the federal estate death tax credit made the NH Estate Tax return unnecessary.

Do I pay transfer tax when a house passes to me by will?

No. Transfer by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death is exempt. When you later sell, the tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, shared by buyer and seller.

What is the federal estate tax threshold in 2026?

The figure is $15,000,000 for a 2026 death. Smaller estates generally owe no federal estate tax.

Where do probate questions go in New Hampshire?

To the Probate Court in the decedent's home county, which is part of the Circuit Court Probate Division.

How long a New Hampshire eviction takes

An eviction here is a short chain of dated steps: a written notice, a court writ, a return day, a hearing within about 10 days of the tenant's appearance, and a writ of possession that issues no sooner than 8 days after a loss at hearing. Add the notice period of 7 or 30 days and you are looking at several weeks from first notice to a sheriff at the door. An appeal or a request for extra time makes it longer.

That arithmetic matters if you own a rented house you want to sell. A buyer who needs the house vacant will ask for a date, and in this process only the court sets it. The sections below walk through the steps in order.

The steps in order

There are nine usual steps, and the first one happens outside the courthouse.

StepWhat happensTiming
1. Eviction noticeLandlord serves a written notice stating the reason7 or 30 days under RSA 540:3
2. WritLandlord files a landlord and tenant writ after the notice expiresSheriff serves the tenant
3. Return dayWrit goes back to the court; tenant files an appearance to contest7 days from service
4. HearingCourt schedules the merits hearingWithin 10 days after an appearance
5. JudgmentCourt issues a written decisionNot always the same day
6. Writ of possessionIssues to the landlord; only a sheriff carries it outNo sooner than 8 days after the hearing
7. Discretionary stayTenant may ask for more timeUp to 90 days if rent is paid weekly
8. Notice of intent to appealFiled at the circuit courtWithin 7 days
9. Supreme Court appealAppeal perfected at the New Hampshire Supreme CourtWithin 30 days

Before the landlord files in court

First the landlord serves the eviction notice and, for nonpayment, a demand for rent listing the unpaid dates and the amount owed. Record the date and time the papers were delivered in a certificate of service.

A nonpayment tenant still has the right to cure. Under RSA 540:9, paying all rent owed through the payment date, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and the landlord's filing and service fees before the merits hearing ends the case, and the landlord must file a receipt with the court. The cure is limited to 3 times in 12 months.

Free remote mediation is also available through the court's Office of Mediation and Arbitration at 603-271-6418. It is an optional step, and it can save both sides a hearing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The landlord and tenant writ and the return day

The writ is the summons that starts the court case. The return day is the date by which the signed writ must be back at the court and the tenant must file an appearance. Under RSA 540:13, the writ is returnable 7 days after the sheriff serves it.

The landlord can file the writ only after the eviction notice has expired, and must attach the expired notice, any demand for rent and the filing fee. A sheriff must serve it. Anyone can serve the eviction notice, but not the writ.

The return day is a filing deadline for the tenant and is not a hearing date. A tenant who files an appearance by then gets a hearing. A tenant who does not may be found in default, after which the court mails a default notice and, if the tenant does not respond, can issue a writ of possession. RSA 540:13 requires the default notice to be mailed at least 3 days before the writ issues.

A newer law also requires the tenant to file an answer within 5 days of the return day. Check the current court forms before relying on the older appearance-only description.

What happens at the hearing?

At the hearing the landlord has to prove the grounds for eviction by a preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely than not, and has to show strict compliance with the notice and, for nonpayment, the demand for rent. When a landlord seeks only possession, the court considers only the defenses set out in RSA 540, such as retaliation or violation of the health and safety standard.

The landlord can also ask for unpaid rent in the same case. The tenant's offsets and counterclaims are then considered, and any money judgment is capped at $1,500 per decision, though either side may sue separately for more (RSA 540:13). The hearing notice must be mailed at least 6 days before the hearing.

The judge may rule from the bench or by mail. If the tenant wins, the tenant stays and the court can award costs. If the landlord wins, a judgment for costs and a writ of possession follow after a short period.

When the tenant has to leave

A tenant has to leave only when a sheriff serves the writ of possession and orders them out, which is never on the day of a lost hearing. The writ does not go to the landlord any sooner than 8 days after the hearing, and the landlord cannot serve it personally.

Two things can stretch the timeline:

  • A discretionary stay: the court may delay the writ for up to 90 days if the tenant keeps paying rent weekly. Ask the clerk what length the court is applying in your case.
  • An appeal: a notice of intent to appeal must be filed within 7 days of the notice of judgment, and the appeal perfected with the Supreme Court within 30 days. In nonpayment cases the tenant pays a weekly amount set by the court during the appeal, and missed payments can bring a default on appeal and the writ of possession.

There is also a pay-and-stay route. A tenant may remain under an agreed schedule of timely payments, and missed payments can lead to eviction without another hearing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Hampshire houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When the landlord lost the house to foreclosure

Even then a judge's permission is required. A tenant renting an apartment or single-family home that the landlord has just lost to foreclosure is entitled to the full process, so a bank that takes the property goes through the same steps.

In practice the tenant process above applies whoever ends up as landlord. Our separate New Hampshire foreclosure guide covers the lender side.

Mistakes that slow an eviction down

Most delays trace to notice errors or to self-help. The same few problems come up again and again:

  • A notice that gives the reason only vaguely, or a nonpayment notice that leaves out the right to cure.
  • Filing the writ before the notice period has fully run.
  • No demand for rent in a nonpayment case.
  • Changing locks, cutting utilities or removing belongings before the sheriff acts. RSA 540-A:3 bars willful lockouts and utility shutoffs without judicial process, and a tenant can file a 540-A petition.
  • Throwing away belongings too fast. The landlord must take reasonable care of a former tenant's property for 7 days after the tenant leaves.

Each of these restarts the clock or exposes the owner to a claim.

Selling a rented house during an eviction

If you would rather not run the process at all, you have a choice. You can finish the court steps and then sell vacant, or you can sell the house with the tenant in place. A buyer who plans to keep it as a rental does not need a sheriff's writ.

Keep the paperwork in one folder: the lease, the notice, the demand for rent, proof of service and any court papers. Whichever path you pick, a buyer or title company will want to see where the case stands.

We buy New Hampshire houses as-is with tenants in place, and a conversation does not commit you to anything.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in New Hampshire?

It varies, but the steps have set limits: a 7 or 30 day notice, a return day 7 days after the writ is served, a hearing within 10 days of the tenant's appearance, and a writ of possession no sooner than 8 days after the hearing. A stay or appeal can add time.

Can a New Hampshire landlord evict without going to court?

No for a typical residential rental. The landlord must get a judge's permission, and only a sheriff can carry out the writ of possession. RSA 540-A:3 bars willful lockouts and utility shutoffs without judicial process.

What is the most a landlord can recover in an eviction case?

The money judgment in a landlord and tenant writ case is capped at $1,500 per decision. Either party can bring a separate suit for more (RSA 540:13).

Can the tenant appeal an eviction?

Yes. The tenant files a notice of intent to appeal within 7 days of the notice of judgment and perfects the appeal with the Supreme Court within 30 days, and keeps paying rent during the appeal.

Is mediation available for New Hampshire evictions?

Yes. The court offers free remote mediation through its Office of Mediation and Arbitration, reachable at 603-271-6418.

New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Where probate happens in New Hampshire

Probate runs through the Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges sitting in courthouses in each of the state's ten counties. The Probate Division handles wills, trusts and estates, guardianships, adoptions, name changes, and equity matters such as partition and quiet title.

Estates that began electronically are e-filed at every probate location. The Circuit Court's single toll-free number is 1-855-212-1234. Contested matters can go to a free probate mediation program, which helps when heirs disagree about whether to keep or sell the house.

The court supervises the estate, while the deed for any sale is recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies.

What are the main steps of a New Hampshire estate?

The court appoints an executor or administrator, who inventories assets, pays debts and distributes what is left. The court's estates self-help page points fiduciaries to its "Administering an Estate" booklet.

  • A will, if there is one, and an application for appointment are filed with the Probate Division.
  • The fiduciary files an Inventory within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1.
  • Debts, funeral costs and administration expenses are paid in the order RSA 554:19 sets.
  • The estate is closed by an accounting, a summary administration, or, for qualifying estates, a waiver of administration.

Estates that require publication of notice pay a publication fee, so ask the clerk for the current amount when you file.

What goes on the inventory when the estate owns a house

List real estate with its address, county, book and page from the Registry of Deeds, and an estimated value. Town tax records may serve as the estimate, an appraiser is not required unless the court orders one, and the amounts need not be exact (see the court's inventory overview).

Values are as of the date of death, and jointly held property is not listed. If the estimate turns out to be significantly off, the fiduciary can file an amended inventory or correct it in the accounting. The total also matters because it can affect the bond the court has already set.

If you plan to sell, a realistic value on the inventory helps later. A sale price far from the inventory figure invites questions from heirs and the court.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can an executor sell the house, and does the court have to approve?

An administrator needs a court license to sell real estate when the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies. RSA 554:17 requires the administrator to apply for the license, and neglecting to do so is treated as maladministration and a breach of the bond.

The court's Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Debts form shows how it works in practice. The fiduciary lists the property by county, book and page, totals the debts and assets, and states the shortfall.

  • The motion asks to sell at public auction or private sale.
  • A surviving spouse can assent to the sale, including the homestead right. If there is no spouse but minor children, a guardian of the minors consents.
  • The order's license is valid for two years from the date of the order.
  • A return of sale goes to the court within one year of the sale, and net proceeds are reported within 30 days of receipt.

Under RSA 554:33, no such license issues later than two years after the executor or administrator was appointed. If the estate has plenty of cash and the will gives the executor power to sell, the path can differ, so ask the court or an attorney which route fits.

Waiver of administration

Waiver of administration is a simplified process under RSA 553:32 that skips the inventory, the fiduciary bond and the accounting. It can help a seller whose estate is small and uncontested. The statute lists who qualifies.

  • A will names one beneficiary who is appointed administrator, or all beneficiaries serve together, or a trust is the sole beneficiary.
  • There is no will and one heir, including a surviving spouse, is appointed, or all heirs serve together or consent to an appropriate person.
  • The court finds waiver appropriate.

The administrator closes the estate by filing an affidavit of administration between 6 months and 1 year after appointment. There is no value cap and real estate is not excluded, but the affidavit has to list all real estate the decedent owned at death, with its location, book and page. It also has to state that, to the administrator's knowledge, there are no outstanding debts.

Waiver does not erase the duty to pay expenses and debts from estate assets. Any interested person may petition for full administration before the affidavit is filed.

How long creditors have to make claims

Creditors work on a short clock once an administrator is appointed. Under RSA 556:1, no action can be sustained against an administrator within six months after the original grant of administration, and not unless the demand has been shown to the administrator. Under RSA 556:5, suit must begin within one year after the original grant, with exceptions where the administrator has retained estate in hand.

Deadline or limitRule
InventoryWithin 90 days after appointment
Waiver affidavit6 months to 1 year after appointment
License to sell real estateNot issued later than 2 years after appointment
License validity2 years from the order
Suit against administratorWithin 1 year of original grant
Creditor action on real estate if no administrationBarred after 2 years from death

RSA 556:29 provides that if no administration was granted within two years of the date of death, no creditor can afterward maintain an action to reach the real estate. The details depend on the facts, so ask an attorney before relying on it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Hampshire houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Inheritance and estate tax on the house

New Hampshire has neither. The Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and the state estate tax return is not required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. The Department of Revenue Administration has a page on both.

The real estate transfer tax also exempts inherited property: transfers by devise, by intestate succession and descent, and by the death of a joint tenant are exceptions. A later sale to a buyer is different. That sale is taxable at $.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller, and each side buys stamps from the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.

The fiduciary deed

The executor or administrator signs a fiduciary deed, which RSA 477:30 sets out in a statutory form. By signing, the fiduciary covenants that he or she was duly authorized to make the sale and followed the statute in doing so. The deed must be acknowledged, and it has to show the grantee's mailing address, under RSA 477:3.

A cash buyer can often work around a slow estate because the sale is as-is and does not depend on a lender's appraisal. The court steps above still apply, though. Before you list or sign, line up these items:

  • The court's appointment papers showing who may sign.
  • A license to sell, if the sale is needed to pay debts.
  • The inventory, so the sale price can be compared with the estimated value.
  • The consent of a surviving spouse or a guardian of minor children, where that is required.

We buy houses in New Hampshire from estates and can coordinate with your attorney on timing. We do not give legal advice.

Frequently asked questions

Which court handles probate in New Hampshire?

The Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges serving courthouses in each of the ten counties. It handles wills, trusts, estates, guardianships and related equity matters.

How soon after appointment must the inventory be filed?

Within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1. The inventory lists real estate with its county, book and page and an estimated fair market value, and town tax records may be used as the estimate.

Does an executor need court permission to sell inherited real estate?

If the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies, an administrator must apply for a license to sell under RSA 554:17. The license is valid for two years, and none issues later than two years after appointment.

Is there a way to skip the inventory and accounting?

Yes, in qualifying cases. Waiver of administration under RSA 553:32 skips the inventory, bond and accounting, and the estate closes with an affidavit filed between 6 months and 1 year after appointment.

Is the transfer tax owed when heirs receive the house?

No. Transfers by devise, intestate succession or the death of a joint tenant are exceptions to the real estate transfer tax. A later sale to a buyer is taxable at $.75 per $100, paid by each side.

content:
New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

No New Hampshire tax on the gain

Selling a house in New Hampshire does not trigger a state tax on your profit. The state taxes no W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax is repealed.

Three other costs remain. The federal government taxes home-sale profit unless an exclusion covers it, the state takes a transfer tax on the deed, and the town expects its share of property tax at closing. Questions about your own return can go to the Department of Revenue Administration Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 or to a tax professional. Treat this page as general information.

  • Income tax: none on wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax is repealed
  • Transfer tax: charged on the deed, shared by buyer and seller
  • Federal: capital gain tax on profit beyond the home sale exclusion
  • Town: property tax prorated or paid at closing

The Interest and Dividends Tax is gone

The Interest and Dividends (I&D) Tax applied to interest and dividend income, and it was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. It never reached the proceeds of a house sale. People confuse it with a capital gains tax because it was New Hampshire's only tax that reached investment income.

Taxable periodI&D Tax rate
Ending before December 31, 20235 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20234 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20243 percent
Beginning after December 31, 2024Repealed

The repeal is covered in Technical Information Release 2025-001, and the law sits in RSA 77 and Rev 900. If you still need to file a final I&D return for an earlier period, file them on Granite Tax Connect.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work?

Federal law shelters $250,000 of profit for a single seller and $500,000 for a married couple filing together, but only on a main home. You qualify by passing two tests.

First test: ownership. Your name must have been on the title for 24 months or more somewhere in the five years before closing. Second test: use. You must have lived there as your residence for 24 months or more in that same stretch. Those months can fall at different times. On a joint return, one spouse's ownership is enough, yet both spouses have to meet the use test.

  • No second exclusion if you took one on another house within the past two years.
  • Received a Form 1099-S? Report the sale, even if all of the profit is excludable.
  • Form 8949 and Schedule D carry the reporting when it is required.
  • Service members, Foreign Service staff and intelligence-community members on qualified extended duty can elect to pause the five-year clock for as long as 10 years.
  • Publication 523 has worksheets, special cases and the full rules.

Taking payments over several years through an installment sale does not cost you the exclusion.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Federal rates on gain above the exclusion

Hold the house for more than a year and the profit is long-term, taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on your taxable income. Sell within a year and it is short-term, taxed at your ordinary rate.

Tax years beginning in 2025 set the brackets this way. Single filers: 0 percent through $48,350, then 15 percent through $533,400, then 20 percent. Joint filers: 0 percent through $96,700, then 15 percent through $600,050, then 20 percent.

Rental history changes things. Any slice of profit traced to unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at no more than 25 percent, which matters if you rented the house and wrote off depreciation. Higher earners may owe the net investment income tax as well, and a big profit can mean estimated payments during the year.

If you sell a personal home at a loss, the loss is not tax deductible.

Inherited or improved homes: figuring the gain

Your taxable gain is the sale proceeds minus adjusted basis. Basis begins at your purchase cost, goes up with improvements that add value, and goes down with things like allowable depreciation.

Gifted and inherited houses follow separate basis rules, found in Publication 551, Basis of Assets. If the house was inherited, get an appraisal for the date of death and keep it with the estate papers. Your preparer will ask for it.

  • Improvements: new roof, additions, major systems. Keep receipts.
  • Selling costs: ask your preparer which closing costs reduce the amount realized.
  • Holding period: Publication 544 covers the special holding-period rules for a house acquired from a decedent.

Transfer tax at closing

Expect a deed tax of $0.75 on each $100 of the price. You pay it, and so does the buyer. A very small sale, $4,000 or less, carries a flat $20 minimum per side. The rules are in RSA 78-B and Rev 800.

Stamps are bought at the county register of deeds, which attaches them when the deed is recorded.

After recording, you have 30 days to send in the paperwork: CD-57-P from the purchaser, CD-57-S from you as seller, and the Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34). Granite Tax Connect accepts the filings and the payment.

  • Taxed: ordinary sales, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds and leases of 99 years or more
  • Exempt: gifts, spousal transfers under a final divorce decree, corrective deeds, transfers to the state, a county or a municipality, and transfers by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Hampshire houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax in a New Hampshire sale

The town's tax year runs from April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), and each bill rests on the April inventory. The owner on April 1 is who the bill names. At closing, the settlement agent splits the year between you and the buyer.

Unpaid taxes build interest at 8 percent (RSA 76:13). When the town records a lien, the rate becomes 14 percent a year under RSA 80:69, and anyone holding a legal interest in the land can redeem before a deed goes to the collector. Expect the title company to pay a lien from your proceeds.

For city specifics, our Manchester and Nashua guides cover those offices and dates.

Before you sell with a large gain

Put numbers on your basis and your exclusion before you sign anything. They decide whether federal tax is due. Someone who lived in the house for two of the past five years and nets under $250,000 may owe nothing federally, though some sales still get reported.

  1. Pull your purchase closing statement and improvement receipts.
  2. Count the months you owned and lived there during the last five years.
  3. Check whether a 1099-S will be issued.
  4. Ask a preparer about estimated tax if a taxable gain is likely.
  5. Budget for the 0.75 percent transfer tax on your side.

A cash sale leaves the tax rules alone. It only moves the calendar, so you can match the day proceeds arrive to any estimated payment your preparer expects. Take your original closing statement, improvement receipts and tax notices to that first meeting.

Frequently asked questions

Does New Hampshire have a capital gains tax?

Not on a home sale. The state taxes no W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Federal tax can still apply.

How much profit can I exclude when I sell my house?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, provided you owned and lived in the house for at least 24 months of the last five years. A prior exclusion on another home within two years rules it out.

Who pays the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax?

The buyer and seller each pay $0.75 per $100 of the price. Transfers through a will, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death are exempt.

Do I report a home sale if I owe no tax?

Yes when a Form 1099-S arrives, even if the gain is fully excludable. Report it as well when part of the gain is taxable.

Can I deduct a loss on my personal home?

No. A loss on personal-use property such as your home is not tax deductible.

New Hampshire Recording a Deed: Fees, Where to File and What to Bring

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Hampshire Recording a Deed sale

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where to record a deed

A deed is recorded with the registry of deeds in the county where the land sits. RSA 477:3-a requires every deed or other conveyance of real estate to be recorded at length there, and until it is, the document has no force against bona fide purchasers for value.

The state has ten county registries: Belknap, Carroll, Cheshire, Coos, Grafton, Hillsborough, Merrimack, Rockingham, Strafford and Sullivan. NHDeeds.org links to each county's site. A parcel that crosses a county line gets recorded in every county it touches.

RSA 477:7 adds that a deed of bargain and sale, a mortgage or another conveyance cannot hold the property against anyone except the grantor and the grantor's heirs unless it is acknowledged and recorded. That is why a closing is not truly finished until the register has the deed in hand.

What a deed needs before the register accepts it

Under RSA 477:3 the grantor signs, and a justice, notary public or commissioner takes the acknowledgment. The deed also has to show the grantee's mailing address. RSA 478:4-a adds more items the register checks.

  • The latest mailing address of each grantee.
  • The name of every municipality where the property lies, in the first sentence of the first description paragraph.
  • The name of each signer, printed or typed under the signature.
  • A document that can be reproduced cleanly under the standards the registers of deeds adopt and post.

RSA 478:4 also calls for paper, markings and a page size that allow suitable permanent recording. The layout standards come from the registers, so call the county office or read its website before you send anything on paper.

A rejected deed delays the whole file, and the buyer's lender will not release funds until recording is certain. Many rejections come from a missing grantee address, an unnamed municipality or a signer's name that is not printed under the signature.

Which type of deed is used for a sale?

New Hampshire has statutory short forms, and a deed that follows one in substance carries the covenants the statute attaches to it. RSA 477:27 covers the warranty deed, RSA 477:28 the quitclaim deed, RSA 477:30 the fiduciary deed, and RSA 477:31 the foreclosure deed under power of sale.

An executor or administrator selling for an estate signs the fiduciary form. In it the grantor covenants that he or she was duly authorized to make the sale and followed the statute. If you inherited the house, our probate page covers the court steps that come first.

Warranty versus quitclaim wording changes what the seller promises about title, so it is a legal call. Your closing attorney can tell you which one fits your sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Hampshire house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees

RSA 478:17-g sets the charge: $10 for the first page and $4 for each additional page, plus a $25 surcharge for the Land and Community Heritage Investment Program (LCHIP). On a deed, the grantee pays that $25.

Recording charges at the registry of deeds
ChargeAmount
Recording a document, first page$10
Each additional recorded page$4
Mortgage discharge or lien release, first page$15, plus $4 each additional page
LCHIP surcharge on each deed, mortgage, discharge or plan (grantee pays on a deed)$25
Plan recording$9 for first 200 square inches, $2.50 per additional 100
Real estate transfer tax, each side$.75 per $100 of price

The surcharge is waived when the United States, the state, a county, a municipality, a village district or a school district is a party. Copies and other services cost whatever each register posts, so ask the office for its current list before you request certified copies of your own deed after closing.

How the transfer tax works at recording

New Hampshire taxes the transfer itself at $.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, and both buyer and seller pay it. Each side buys stamps from the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, the register affixes them to the deed, and the deed is then recorded.

  • When the consideration is $4,000 or less, the minimum is $20 from each side.
  • Related-party transfers with unsupported stated prices are taxed on fair market value.
  • Foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds and easements are taxable transfers.
  • Exceptions include transfers by devise or intestate succession, transfers on the death of a joint tenant, and transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree.

Within 30 days after recording, each side files a Declaration of Consideration (Form CD-57-P for the buyer, CD-57-S for the seller) and an Inventory of Property Transfer (Form PA-34) with the Department of Revenue Administration. Filers use its Granite Tax Connect portal. Manufactured housing and trusts follow their own transfer tax rules, so ask the closing attorney if either applies.

Can you record a deed electronically?

In principle, yes. New Hampshire adopted the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act, effective February 6, 2022 (RSA 478-A), and RSA 478-A:3 covers the validity of electronic documents and the recording of tangible copies of them.

Each county registry handles e-recording in its own way, so confirm with the register before counting on a same-day record. Most sellers never file the deed themselves. The closing attorney or title company does it.

A typical recording day runs in order. The deed is signed and acknowledged at the closing table. Both sides pay the transfer tax and the stamps go on the deed. The register records it, charges the page fees and the LCHIP surcharge, and the forms for the Department of Revenue Administration follow within 30 days. As seller, you mainly need to be sure your side of the stamps and your CD-57-S are handled.

If you are selling for cash, ask early who will record, what it will cost, and when the stamps will be bought. Check the grantee address, the municipality names and the printed signer names before closing day, since the register will refuse a deed that lacks them.

Manufactured homes and trusts

The transfer tax treats these differently. For manufactured housing, tax on most transfers goes to the register of deeds in the county where the unit is located, paid by both buyer and seller. A unit moving into New Hampshire from another state is taxed to the buyer alone, and one moving out of the state is taxed to the seller alone.

A transfer into a revocable trust is taxable unless an exception applies, though the tax can be the minimum when the trust is set up for estate planning as a testamentary substitute and the transfer is between the trust and its grantor. Transfers to or from an irrevocable trust are not taxable if the elements of a gift are met or an exception applies.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in New Hampshire?

With the registry of deeds in the county where the land lies. Under RSA 477:3-a, an unrecorded deed has no effect against bona fide purchasers for value.

How much does recording cost?

$10 for the first page and $4 for each additional page, plus a $25 LCHIP surcharge on each deed, which the grantee pays. Transfer tax is separate.

What is the transfer tax rate?

$.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, owed by both the buyer and the seller. Each side buys stamps from the register of deeds.

What forms are filed after recording?

Each side files a Declaration of Consideration (CD-57-P or CD-57-S) and an Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) within 30 days after recording.

Is inherited property subject to transfer tax?

Transfers by devise, intestate succession or the death of a joint tenant are exceptions. A later sale of the house by the heir is taxable.
